questions.question: What is the Harvest Derivation Law and what does it say about harvest scripts?
questions.expected_key: n-gram keys AIML patterns and Node Field Graph vertices are all derived from @transpile productions not hand-authored per section harvest scripts are a transitional compiler pass over the grammar target architecture is a grammar compiler that emits all three directly from @transpile grammar is single source of truth harvest scripts are temporary bridge

questions.question: What is the difference between Aho-Corasick and the harvest compiler pass — are they the same operation?
questions.expected_key: No. AC is a runtime recognition backend: it scans input text at query time answers WHERE a surface form matched O(n+m+z). Harvest scripts are a compile-time compiler pass: they read @transpile productions from the grammar and emit n-gram keys AIML patterns NFG vertices before any query runs. AC consumes what harvest produced. They are at opposite ends of the pipeline: harvest is source-time grammar-to-artifacts, AC is query-time text-to-key. Conflating them is the MISS: AC does NOT perform harvest derivation.
questions.miss_source: Gemma1B conflated AC with harvest derivation because both appear in the §71 AC Subordination and Harvest Derivation laws in the same context block

questions.question: Does Aho-Corasick perform canonicalization, or does it trigger it?
questions.expected_key: AC triggers canonicalization but does not perform it. AC returns position and surface_form to the grammar runtime. The grammar runtime then applies the canonicalization attribute declared in @transpile. They are separate pipeline phases even if run back-to-back in a single pass. AC is a replaceable recognition backend. Canonicalization is a grammar-defined rule. AC is the trigger; grammar runtime is the actor.
questions.miss_source: LFM said 'AC performs canonicalization during the recognition phase' — blurring the phase boundary between recognition and canonicalization

questions.question: What three projection attributes must every @transpile production declare, and what space does each live in?
questions.expected_key: b(addr) positions the key in FQ_n binary topology (discrete n-bit). theta(face) assigns a C_6 phase Pop/Wo/Yax/Sek/Ch_en/Xul (discrete 6-state cyclic). gram(ref) points to the manifest book for continuous geometry g in R^m. All three are required. Omitting b means no binary address in the folded hypercube. Listing only theta and g as geometric descriptors is a MISS — b is not optional.
questions.miss_source: LFM enumerated @transpile as surface_forms + canonical_key + 'theta and g' — dropped b from the projection triple

jokes.pattern: WHY DOES KUHUL USE AHO CORASICK INSTEAD OF TRYING ONE PATTERN AT A TIME
jokes.punchline: Because trying one pattern at a time is backtracking over the token stream, and we already have a whole section in the grammar about why backtracking is O(2^n). Aho-Corasick builds the dictionary into a trie, scans once, and hands you all the matches. Then K'UHUL decides which ones matter. Fast recognition first, slow reasoning later — not the other way around.

jokes.pattern: WHAT DOES THE FAILURE LINK DO IN PLAIN LANGUAGE
jokes.punchline: It says: you were hoping to match the long key but you failed partway through. Here is the longest shorter key that still makes sense given what you have already seen. It is the algorithm's version of SC-37: when the ambitious match fails, do not restart from zero — retain the most informative suffix you managed to recognize.

jokes.pattern: WHY IS AN NGRAM AN ADDRESS AND NOT A PROBABILITY
jokes.punchline: Because probabilities tell you how often. Addresses tell you where. You do not look up 'deliver the pitch' in a probability table and get back a neighborhood. You look it up in a key grammar and get back a book — a semantic neighborhood full of setup, performance, context, and payoff. The n-gram is the key. The book is what it opens.

jokes.pattern: IS AN NGRAM THE SAME AS THE FIELD IN KUHUL
jokes.punchline: No. The n-gram is the address. The field is the neighborhood you get when you look it up. Saying the n-gram is the field is like saying a street address is the building. The address tells you where to find the building. The building is everything you encounter once you arrive — all the rooms, the neighbors, the connections, the history. Recognize the key first. Then unfold the field. Do not confuse the postal code with the city.

jokes.pattern: WHAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A TRIE EDGE AND A KEY BOOK EDGE
jokes.punchline: A trie edge says: after seeing this prefix, transition to this state. A key book edge says: this key is semantically adjacent to this other concept. One is recognition machinery. The other is meaning. You need both: the trie to find the key, the book to know what the key means. Aho-Corasick builds the trie. K'UHUL maintains the books.

jokes.pattern: WHY DOES AHO-CORASICK CHOOSE THE AC AUTOMATON OVER A SIMPLE PATTERN MATCH
jokes.punchline: Because it avoids the tedious backtracking of one pattern at a time.

jokes.pattern: WHEN THE N-GRAM KEY IS TREATED AS AN ADDRESS, IT TRANSFORMS THE SEARCH SPACE INT
jokes.punchline: It turns structural fallback into a well-organized database of meanings.

jokes.pattern: IN THE NODE FIELD GRAPH, EVERY ADDRESS MAPS TO A SEMANTIC NODE—NO MORE GUESSING
jokes.punchline: So the failure link becomes a clever structural fallback, not a dead end.

jokes.pattern: THE BAG-OF-KEYS ALGORITHM CAPTURES OVERLAPPING MATCHES, ENRICHING THE SEMANTIC B
jokes.punchline: Thus, n-grams become addresses in the semantic book, not just random strings.
